title: Diagnosing and Correcting Reward Hacking in Verifiable Instruction Following
location: Sec. 3 (evaluation blind spot), Fig. 3; also Sec. 5.3, Table 2
quote: in all three matched OLMo 3 (Olmo et al., 2025) DPO–RLVR pairs, the RLVR checkpoint achieves higher Constraint Satisfaction but lower Response Quality
measures: IFBench loose constraint satisfaction vs mean 1-10 Response Quality from three frontier LLM judges, for OLMo 3 DPO vs RLVR checkpoints (7B Instruct, 7B Think, 32B Think; 3.0 vs 3.1 not stated) and own IF-RLVR runs (Qwen3 1.7B/4B, Tulu 3 8B); pass@1-level means; on base-fail to trained-pass prompts IF-RLVR quality drops 2.05 points.
reason: Same phenomenon, same benchmark, same model family (OLMo3-32B Think DPO to RLVR): RL passes with less substantive answers. But it reports mean judge scores at pass@1, not the share of verified successes that are gamed, and does not tie gaming to reach at large k or to prompts the start never solves.

title: Generalizing Verifiable Instruction Following
location: Sec. 5 (Reward Hacking and the Instruction Hierarchy); Fig. 7; App. E
quote: Completions from the base policy are scored higher by the LLM-as-judge than completions from the IF-RLVR trained model
measures: GPT-4.1 judge 1-10 rating (constraints removed) of IFEval/IFBench completions from the base policy vs their IF-RLVR model (avg 7.0 vs 6.4); Fig. 7 shows a keyword-stuffing over-optimized output; no fraction of gamed passes, no pass@k.
reason: IFBench authors flag over-optimization (constraint over task, keyword stuffing) and a mean judge-quality drop at pass@1; they do not quantify gamed successes or connect them to reach.

title: IFDecorator: Wrapping Instruction Following Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards
location: Introduction; Trip Wire section (Macro Hack Rate, Eq. 5)
quote: trip wires reveal that IntentCheck significantly reduces the reward hacking rate from 14.53% to 7.60%
measures: Macro Hack Rate = share of trap (trip-wire) instructions whose response matches rule-coded exploit patterns (placeholder copying, dummy lists, repetition, delimiter copying), for Qwen2.5-7B/32B-Instruct and Qwen3-8B IF-RLVR with vs without IntentCheck; single responses.
reason: Quantifies IF reward hacking, but on purpose-built trap prompts as a training diagnostic, not among the benchmark successes that decide a start-vs-RL reach comparison.

title: Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards Implicitly Incentivizes Correct Reasoning in Base LLMs
location: Sec. 5 (Training Dynamics of RLVR, Limitations of DAPO); App. A.6
quote: we can still observe a non-negligible portion of imperfect CoTs (the median of P (CC|CA)(q) is around 0.7)
measures: LLM verifier (DeepSeek-R1-0528-Qwen3-8B; any/all/majority of repeated verifications) on every correct-answer sample: CoT-Pass@K for Qwen2.5-32B vs DAPO-Qwen-32B on AIME24/25, MATH-500, AMC23, Minerva to k=1024; P(CC|CA) per training question during DAPO.
reason: Maths analogue of C4: answer-checker pass@k counts flawed-reasoning successes (mainly on the base side at large k; RL-side median P(CC|CA) about 0.7 on training questions). Same move of filtering the successes that decide the boundary, but maths and flawed CoTs, not IF checker gaming.

title: Does Reinforcement Learning Really Incentivize Reasoning Capacity in LLMs Beyond the Base Model?
quote: Similarly, the RL-trained model answered 6 questions, 4 of which included at least one correct CoT.
measures: Manual check of every correct CoT on the hardest solved problems (mean accuracy below 5%) for base vs SimpleRL-Zoo models: GSM8K (base 24/25, RL 23/25 problems with a valid CoT) and guess-filtered AIME24 (base 5/6, RL 4/6); large-k sampling.
reason: Hand-audits the successes that decide a large-k boundary comparison on both sides and reports the genuine share (RL 4 of 6 AIME24 problems). Maths, tiny counts, not blinded, not IF gaming.

title: LLMs Gaming Verifiers: RLVR can Lead to Reward Hacking
location: Sec. 4 (Monitoring Shortcut Behaviour; RLVR optimization pressure), Tab. 1
quote: olmo-3.1 trained under the same setup but with extended RLVR optimization begins to exhibit shortcuts
measures: Isomorphic Perturbation Testing on SLR-Bench inductive-logic tasks (one output per task): count of outputs passing extensional verification but failing isomorphic verification, for GPT-5 family, OLMo-3/3.1 7B/32B and non-RLVR models; plus controlled RLVR of Olmo-3-7B-Think-DPO.
reason: Counts checker-passing but non-genuine outputs and finds them in the same RL lineage (OLMo-3.1 32B, not OLMo-3 32B); inductive logic at pass@1, not IF and not a reach measurement.

title: Is Your Code Generated by ChatGPT Really Correct? Rigorous Evaluation of Large Language Models for Code Generation
quote: catch significant amounts of previously undetected wrong code synthesized by LLMs, reducing the pass@k by up-to 19.3-28.9%
measures: Re-graded HumanEval samples of many LLMs against 80x more tests (HumanEval+): pass@1/10/100 fall by 19.3/24.9/28.9%.
reason: Classic evidence that checker-only pass@k overstates success, more so at larger k; code with weak tests rather than gaming; no RL-vs-start reach.

title: Olmo 3
location: RL findings: Mixing RL data from varied domains can prevent over-optimization (Fig. 20-21)
quote: the LM-judge reward ensures that the model continues to produce well-formed chat responses
measures: OlmoRL ablations: IFEval-only RL trades off AlpacaEval; final mixed RL (with an LM-judge reward) keeps AlpacaEval; lower train reward on mixed data read as less reward hacking.
reason: The developers expect the mixed recipe to curb IF over-optimization but measure no gaming among successes; in tension with C4 (and with 2610.19525), not a comparable measurement.

title: Same Answer, New Box: How Much of RLVR's Out-of-Domain Gain Is Answer Format?
quote: The base models already state most of their answers in text, and RL moves them into the box
measures: Re-scored stored outputs of four 7B SimpleRL base-RL pairs and one 32B pair on out-of-domain multiple choice with harness extractors vs a text-or-box extractor and blinded LLM readers; 82% (readers 77%) of the reported pass@1 gain is answer format.
reason: Characterises why the start model fails on items RL gains (answer present but not boxed: format), the kind of breakdown C6 makes; but pass@1 OOD multiple choice after maths RL, not IF reach prompts at k=256, and the dominant category is the opposite of ours.

title: Decomposing Elements of Problem Solving: What "Math" Does RL Teach?
location: Sec. 4 (Easy to Plan but Hard to Execute; Partial Repair via GRPO), Figs. 4-5
quote: GRPO significantly reduces both elementary-level math errors and basic logic mistakes
measures: GPT-4.1-mini labels (spot-checked by hand) of plan validity and execution/factual/logic errors in 64 samples per MATH-500 problem for Qwen2.5 0.5B-7B before and after GRPO; coverage wall at pass@64.
reason: Classifies the start model's failure types and which ones GRPO repairs (execution slips, not knowledge), pooled over all generations; not restricted to prompts RL newly solves; maths, not IF.

title: When Pass@k Crossovers Are Real - and Why: Paired Inference and the Markov Kernel of RLVR (v1 title: RLVR is a Kernel, Not a Function: Statistical Inference for pass@k Crossovers)
location: Sec. 5.2 (Forensic anatomy of the locked minority), Fig. 4b
quote: rules out token-limit truncation, formatting failures, or verifier false negatives
measures: Audit of all 4,224 RL completions on 33+22 locked prompts (base solves, RL never does) for DeepScaleR/ProRL at 16k-32k tokens: natural termination, parsed boxed answers, manual plus symbolic re-check, collapse onto a modal wrong answer.
reason: Failure-mode characterisation of the losing side on boundary prompts (substantive modal wrong answers, not truncation/format/verifier misses), but in the reverse direction (RL failing base-solved prompts) and in maths.

title: When Pass@k Crossovers Are Real - and Why: Paired Inference and the Markov Kernel of RLVR (v1 title: RLVR is a Kernel, Not a Function: Statistical Inference for pass@k Crossovers)
location: Sec. 6.2 (Direct measurement to k = 4096 on 3,000 new problems); Sec. 3 paired inference
quote: on the 700 hard-tail problems with at most 8 successes in 256 under at least one model, we drew 4,096 fresh generations per model
measures: Paired prompt-level bootstrap on D(k)=pass@k(RL)-pass@k(base) for nine public RLVR checkpoints (1,060 competition problems, 32k tokens) and own GRPO/SFT arms on 3,000 new problems: Stage 1 n=256, Stage 2 4,096 fresh draws per model on prompts with at most 8/256 under either model; split-half tests; Holm adjustment.
reason: Closest prior for symmetric confirmation: candidates picked by one rule under either model and re-drawn fresh for both, with multiplicity control. Maths only, answer-checker grading, no blinded reader gate, no IF.

title: Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards Implicitly Incentivizes Correct Reasoning in Base LLMs
quote: we manually inspect cases where the Pass@K metric yields a small positive value, but the CoT-Pass@K metric returns zero
measures: LLM-as-a-CoT-judge gate on every correct-answer sample for base and RL (Qwen2.5-32B vs DAPO-Qwen-32B), AIME24/25, MATH-500, AMC23, Minerva to k=1024, with hand inspection of cases the gate zeroes; motivated by easily guessed simple answers.
reason: A model-reader gate on the candidate successes of a boundary study, applied identically to both models (implicitly blind), plus a hand check and the guessing rationale; maths, not IF, no fresh-draw confirmation.

title: Does Reinforcement Learning Really Incentivize Reasoning Capacity in LLMs Beyond the Base Model?
location: App. C.2 (Validity of Chain-of-Thought on AIME24); Sec. 2 Random Guessing Issue
quote: If a problem can be answered correctly with a low but non-zero probability (e.g., <5%), we consider it to be guessable and remove it.
measures: Removes guessable AIME24 problems (30 to 18) by sampling direct no-CoT answers from Qwen2.5-7B-Base; hand-checks correct CoTs of base and RL on the hardest problems; drops multiple-choice items from visual benchmarks.
reason: The standard boundary paper already estimates an empirical guessing baseline on AIME integer answers and hand-gates both sides; any novelty is in the specific estimate, blinding, and symmetry rule.

title: Beyond Pass@k: Breadth-Depth Metrics for Reasoning Boundaries
quote: Pass@k at large k may eventually produce correct answers for all problems, due to random guessing rather than reasoning ability
measures: Pass@k vs Cover@tau (share of problems with per-problem success at least tau) for Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct and RLVR variants on OMEGA and Reasoning Gym, about 8k samples per problem; OMEGA Probability set has 30 possible answers so the base reaches pass@k=1.
reason: Names guessing on small numeric answer spaces as the large-k confound and corrects with a reliability threshold rather than a guessing baseline; does not treat AIME's 0-999 space explicitly.

title: Keep Guessing? When Considering Inference Scaling, Mind the Baselines
quote: we define a baseline that enumerates answers according to their prevalence in the training set
measures: Coverage (pass@k up to k=1,000) of repeated sampling vs a TrainCounts answer-enumeration baseline and a Mixture(M) sample-then-guess baseline on MATH and EntityQuestions for Llama-3, Gemma, Pythia.
reason: Explicit guessing baseline for large-k coverage on skewed small answer sets; predates the RL boundary debate; not RL vs start, not AIME.

title: Same Answer, New Box: How Much of RLVR's Out-of-Domain Gain Is Answer Format?
location: Abstract; Sec. 4.3 and appendix (Blinding and readers)
quote: A reported gain is partly a property of the extractor that read it, and re-scoring stored outputs with a second extractor shows how much
measures: Second extractor beside harness extractors on stored base/RL outputs (OOD multiple choice, five base-RL pairs) plus two blinded LLM readers (no key, no model identity) with a third as tie-breaker; pass@1.
reason: Same methodological move as a second grade beside the RL grader, with a blinded model-reader check; but pass@1 accuracy gains on multiple choice, not reach candidates at large k.

title: From Accuracy to Robustness: A Study of Rule- and Model-based Verifiers in Mathematical Reasoning
quote: Model-based verifiers substantially improve static accuracy but are highly susceptible to reward hacking during RL
measures: Recall/precision of rule-based verifiers (e.g. Math-Verify) and model-based verifiers on maths outputs, and hacking of model verifiers during RL (Qwen2.5 models).
reason: Shows grader choice moves measured correctness (rule-checker false negatives, model-verifier false positives); not a pass@k boundary or start-vs-RL reach audit.
